Empirical Research Plan  
“Bank Durability, Bank Failures, and Borrower Outcomes”

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred design: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension (i.e., staggered DID à la Callaway-Sant’Anna 2021 / Sun-Abraham 2021).  

Why it fits  
• Treatment is a discrete, plausibly exogenous shock—the moment a borrower’s primary bank enters FDIC receivership, is subject to a formal enforcement action, or breaches regulatory capital ratios.  
• Borrowers tied to banks that do **not** experience distress in the sample period form a natural counterfactual.  
• Timing is staggered: different banks fail in different quarters → modern DID estimators handle heterogenous timing and treatment effects.  
• The event-study format lets us visualise pre-trends (key for credibility) and the dynamic pattern of borrower outcomes after the shock.

Optional add-on: Instrumental-variable intensity design (“share of credit from distressed banks” instrumented by branch-level exposure to past failures in the borrower’s county) as a robustness exercise, but the core design is DID.

================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated_i,t = 1 if borrower i’s primary lending bank j experiences “distress event” in quarter τ and t ≥ τ.  
Definition of “distress event”:  
• FDIC receivership OR  
• Formal PCA “Prompt Corrective Action” order OR  
• Tier-1 capital ratio < 4 % (well-capitalized cut-off) for two consecutive quarters.

Control group  
Borrowers whose primary lender never crosses any of the above distress thresholds during the full sample window.

Treatment timing / event date  
Quarter τ in which the first qualifying regulatory event occurs. Relative event-time indicator k = t – τ (…,–2,–1,0,+1,+2,…).

Notes  
• Primary lender identified as the bank with >50 % of borrower i’s outstanding credit during the baseline year.  
• Multi-bank borrowers: create an “exposure share” variable; main regressions use a binary treatment; robustness uses continuous exposure.

================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of a bank distress event, outcomes of treated and control borrowers would have evolved similarly.  
– Plausibility: Borrowers do not pick banks based on forecast of future failure; we will test visually and statistically (event-study coefficients for k < 0 should be ≈ 0).

A2. No anticipatory behaviour: Borrowers cannot perfectly foresee bank failure; there is no large shift in outcomes immediately **before** τ.  
– Regulatory take-over dates are difficult to predict; we still check for “anticipation blips” at k = –1.

A3. SUTVA / no spillovers: Distress of Bank j does not materially affect borrowers linked only to other banks.  
– Could be violated via local credit-market contagion; we mitigate by excluding borrowers operating in the same county as a failed bank but borrowing elsewhere (robustness).

A4. Composition stability: Entry/exit of borrowers is not driven by treatment in a way that biases estimates.  
– Use borrower fixed effects and re-weighting; test for differential attrition.

================================================================
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends or selection into failing banks.  
– Mitigation: Propensity-score or Mahalanobis matching on pre-event characteristics; include borrower*industry and bank*year FE; pre-trend tests.

T2. Macro or regional shocks correlated with bank failure (e.g., local housing bust).  
– Mitigation: County-quarter fixed effects; robustness restricting to multi-state banks (less tied to local shocks); triple-difference using within-county non-relationship firms.

T3. Spillovers & credit reallocation.  
– Mitigation: Exclude borrowers in same 3-digit zip code whose banks remain healthy; alternatively, instrument borrower-level change in credit line with distance-weighted exposure to bank branches of failed banks.

================================================================
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)          # fast high-dim FE estimators
library(did)             # Callaway-Sant'Anna DID
library(modelsummary)    # nice tables

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
borrowers <- read_csv("borrower_financials.csv")   # firm-quarter panel
banks     <- read_csv("bank_events.csv")           # bank-quarter panel

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct treatment
# 2a. Flag bank-level distress date
banks <- banks %>%
  group_by(bank_id) %>%
  mutate(distress = (fdic_failure==1 | pca_order==1 | tier1_capital<0.04),
         distress_quarter = ifelse(distress, quarter, NA)) %>%
  fill(distress_quarter, .direction = "downup")

# 2b. Merge to borrowers via primary_bank_id
panel <- borrowers %>%
  left_join(banks %>% select(bank_id, quarter, distress_quarter), 
            by = c("primary_bank_id" = "bank_id", "quarter")) %>%
  group_by(firm_id) %>%
  mutate(event_time = quarter - distress_quarter,
         treated    = ifelse(!is.na(distress_quarter) & quarter >= distress_quarter, 1, 0),
         ever_treated = ifelse(!is.na(distress_quarter), 1, 0)) %>%
  ungroup()

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID (two-way FE, homogeneous treatment effect)
did_main <- feols(outcome_y ~ treated | firm_id + quarter, data = panel, 
                  cluster = ~primary_bank_id)
etable(did_main)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham style)
panel <- panel %>% mutate(rel_time = ifelse(ever_treated==1, event_time, -999))

event_es <- feols(outcome_y ~ i(rel_time, ever_treated, ref = -1) | 
                    firm_id + quarter, data = panel %>% filter(rel_time >= -8 & rel_time <= 8),
                  cluster = ~primary_bank_id)
iplot(event_es, xlab = "Quarters relative to bank distress", main = "Event study")

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness check: matched sample
# Propensity score based on pre-event size, leverage, relationship length
pre_vars <- c("log_assets", "leverage", "relationship_years")
ps     <- glm(ever_treated ~ ., data = panel %>% 
                filter(quarter==min(quarter)) %>% select(all_of(pre_vars), ever_treated),
              family = binomial)$fitted.values
panel$pscore <- ps[match(panel$firm_id, (panel %>% filter(quarter==min(quarter)))$firm_id)]

matched <- panel %>% filter(abs(pscore - .5) < .4)   # crude caliper demo

did_matched <- feols(outcome_y ~ treated | firm_id + quarter, data = matched,
                     cluster = ~primary_bank_id)
etable(did_main, did_matched)
```

================================================================
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Theory suggests negative borrower consequences: the sudden withdrawal of credit and relationship-specific information raises financing costs and reduces investment.

Priors  
• Investment (CAPEX / assets) ↓ by 5–10 %.  
• Interest expense / debt ↑ by ≈ 75 bp.  
• Probability of borrower financial distress (Altman Z-Score < cutoff or Chapter 11 filing) ↑ by 2–3 pp in the three years post-event.

================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends visually/statistically supported ….. 0.8  
C2. No anticipation (k = –1 insign.)  ………………………………………. 0.7  
C3. No spillovers/contamination …………………………………………. 0.6  
C4. Stable composition / no differential attrition ………………. 0.7  
C5. Correct timing & definition of treatment …………………….. 0.9  

Average ≈ 0.74 → generally credible but not bullet-proof; main weaknesses are potential spillovers and imperfect anticipation.

================================================================
This plan provides a transparent, modern DID framework, several robustness checks, and a clear path to estimating the causal effect of bank durability on borrower financial outcomes.
